body_text: It took several hours longer than expected, but the SS United States is now sitting at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico just off the Florida coast near Pensacola. Rather than serving meals of caviar and roast duck as it did during its heyday zipping across the Atlantic, it will now form an artificial reef that attracts marlin and swordfish, and eventually with them, divers and fishermen, the Associated Press reports . The SS US was larger than the Titanic and set a transatlantic speed record on its first voyage in 1952 with an average speed of 41 miles per hour. Federal rules prevent the use of explosives in intentional scuttlings, so instead Coleen Marine, the company tasked with the sinking, removed the tanks that held seawater used to cool the ship’s boilers. Once water flowed in through the intakes, it flooded the vessel. Over 400 portholes were also removed and large holes cut into the deck. The SS US joins more than 500 other artificial reefs in the area off the Gulf coast where it now lays. Stocks fell on Thursday as Nvidia fell before recovering much of its losses and the AI trade showed resilience despite the ouster of one of the most important CEOs in the industry. In a turn of events that would have been shocking even a week ago, Jensen Huang is out as the CEO of Nvidia after his position leading the most important chipmaker in the world became untenable following the development of a series of scandals about his conduct. The move comes at a major inflection point in the AI trade, after several months of the biggest names from Intel to the AI labs to the neoclouds being rattled by earnings, the debt market, and somewhat ambiguous vibes around the ultimate value of this technology and the ultimate ability of the companies involved in the AI trade to capture it. Huang had long been the sector’s biggest cheerleader, its financier, and the guy responsible for selling the single most valuable piece of hardware technology in the whole boom. The coming weeks will reveal precisely how necessary Huang is to the action here. Consider it a fundamental test of the “great man theory of history” as it applies to business. Was Nvidia successful because of Huang’s particular vision and networking ability? Or will Nvidia be able to continue its run absent its leather-jacketed leader, because at this point it’s not exactly rocket science selling a GPU to a data center. The manner of Huang’s departure will at the very least likely be bruising for Nvidia in the short- to medium-term; the scandal began when it was reported that Huang was engaged in a romantic entanglement with a woman who had been identified as a likely Chinese intelligence asset. The incident that precipitated his actual departure — reporting that indicated this sort of behavior was not exactly exceptional, and that Huang had allegedly been involved with co-workers too — doesn’t exactly paint a great picture. Either way, now Congress is getting involved , as House investigators tend to hate it when the businessman behind the single most important piece of technology of the decade gets honeypotted by America’s primary geopolitical and industrial rival. Nvidia shares took it on the chin this week, but retail traders appear to be bullish on the company’s ability to perform well absent Huang. According to my colleague Luke Kawa and the EntryPoint newsletter , traders have been enthusiastically buying the dip here in anticipation that, however things shake out with Huang, people are going to need those graphics cards and they’re probably fine buying them from Colette Kress for the time being. Indeed, one plausible fallout of this stands to benefit the large firms helming the AI industry in the United States. The frontier labs have long argued that tough regulation of AI, especially the open-source AI that dominates China’s role in the emerging tech, is a necessity. Huang opposed that, through his desire to export his chips to whoever would buy them and his support of the open source world of models and his purchase of HuggingFace. Just a couple of months or so after a Times piece broke the news that Letterboxd — a social media network where ~30 million users log and review movies they’ve watched — had been attracting takeover interest from a host of names in the entertainment industry, it seems that the Grey Lady herself is now leading the charge. Last week, the NYT reported that its parent company had entered into advanced talks to buy the platform for around $330 million. Letterboxd reps and The New York Times Company chose to take non-speaking roles in the report, though sources close to the discussions were on hand to add color. Apparently, Sony Pictures and ever-popular artsy production house A24 had both been circling the platform, with the latter dropping out as the potential takeover bids rose. For its part in the now exclusive negotiations, the Times Company has reportedly discussed keeping Matthew Buchanan and Karl von Randow at the helm, the pair having launched Letterboxd together at a Brooklyn web conference in 2011 . At the time, the final installment in the Harry Potter movie franchise was topping the box office. The media landscape has changed a bit since. For instance, never has the artist’s eternal “everyone’s a critic” complaint been truer, as platforms like Letterboxd and the Amazon -owned Goodreads have almost gamified art consumption; films are something to log, books are something to shelve. Just looking at Letterboxd’s analytics gives you a decent picture of how the business of letting cinephiles record and review their latest watches has boomed in recent years. Given how user figures have ballooned since the pandemic era, with each metric in Letterboxd’s annual year-end review rising at least four times from 2020 to 2025, it’s little wonder that some within the industry have started to refer to younger fervent film fans as the “ Letterboxd Generation .” The rising popularity of platform features such as “ Four Favorites ,” now a mainstay question for celebs stopped on red carpets and stuck in press junkets, as well as getting one of the biggest names in media onboard, makes it hard to imagine a world where Letterboxd users aren’t logging 1 billion+ movies on the platform each year at some point in the near future. As The New York Times Company’s metamorphosis from a news peddler to games-entertainment-product reviews-and-recipes behemoth that runs a side gig sending reporters to war zones continues, deals like this only make more sense. In fairness, the company behind America’s paper of record has provided much more than the news for a while now, having long realized that it needs more than straight reporting to keep modern audiences engaged (and paying up) in the digital age. Indeed, just like Letterboxd hopes that the financial backing and increased visibility from any potential sale will help juice their user numbers and boost its revenue, the Times likely views the Letterboxd deal — like the acquisitions of Wordle and The Athletic before it — as another potential stepping stone towards its goal to 15 million subscribers by the end of 2027. 🏈 NFL: It’s an NFC East showdown tonight between the Washington Commanders and the New York Giants, with New York a 57% favorite . body_text: As companies like DoorDash , Uber and Amazon race to deliver packages and burritos via drones, an unlikely competitor is giving them a run for their money: a chimpanzee sanctuary in Florida . After heavy rains flooded the sanctuary's roads, staff turned to a drone to deliver food to Kaleb, a 38-year-old chimpanzee stranded by the rising waters. His order? A paper bag full of bananas, with some blankets thrown in. Kaleb enjoyed his airborne meal before eventually making his way across the water on a rope. No word on whether he tipped. Hims’ margins, not unlike many of its customers, are getting slimmer. Can peptides help it get back to profit growth? Both Eli Lilly and Novo (formerly known as Novo Nordisk ) reported sales numbers that beat estimates and hiked their outlooks. Earlier this year, both companies released oral GLP-1s that have by all accounts been flying off the pharmacy shelves without cannibalizing sales from its legacy injectable products. Over the years, Lilly and Novo have increasingly sold the drugs through direct-to-consumer channels, often through partnerships with telehealth companies like Hims & Hers. Hims used to sell knock-off versions of Novo’s injectable drugs, which were produced in compounding pharmacies (some owned by Hims, others through partnerships) and officially marketed as bespoke treatments. After more than a year of threats and a brief legal battle with Novo, Hims no longer sells those high-margin knock-offs. Now, it offers Novo and Lilly’s branded drugs on its platforms, which carry significantly lower margins. The company’s profits have taken a hit as a result. On Monday it reported a surprise loss for the quarter along with sales and subscriber count numbers that missed expectations. It also cut its outlook for the year. “We had, as you all saw in the last quarter or two, just a massive transformation of the business, moving from the compounding offerings to the partnership with Novo,” Hims CEO Andrew Dudum told analysts on Monday. Hims also said it will begin offering some unapproved peptide treatments this month after US regulators eased restrictions. Dudum said the new offering will include glutathione, NAD, sermorelin and B12, with BPC-157 and TB-500 potentially coming later, subject to regulatory approval. For the unacquainted, peptides are under-studied supplements , usually injectable, that have grown in popularity in recent years because of their purported health benefits. As of now, consumers are bypassing the FDA by buying vials of peptides labeled “for research use only” and then conducting that research on themselves. Importantly for Hims: the company can sell these treatments while controlling much of the supply chain, from manufacturing to distribution. While it’s unclear how big the market truly is, peptides could offer the kind of attractive margins Hims enjoyed when it was selling compounded GLP-1s. Hims has already acquired a peptide manufacturing facility in Menlo Park, California, and says it's seen a “tremendous amount of excitement” from customers on its waitlist, per Dudum. But the company isn't expecting the new business to contribute meaningfully to revenue in the current quarter. Hims does best when it behaves like a drugmaker , selling its own products versus made in an industrial pharmacy rather than serving as the sleek, neutral colored liaison between you and an actual pharmaceutical company. Selling compounded GLP-1s was very lucrative for Hims. Peptides could give it another shot at that business model. But the company is once again betting on a category where the regulatory ground is still shifting beneath its feet. “In healthcare, whoever owns the customer relationship wins,” Dudum said.
